Subject: Please read and share: fake blue pills and what to do in an emergency

I’m putting this in a separate post because the police warning is important and I don’t want it getting lost under rumours and arguments about Saturday. I’m not going to discuss anyone involved, and I’d ask people not to do that here either.

The police are warning about blue tablets being sold as diazepam or “Xanax”. Some have been found to contain nitazenes, which are synthetic opioids and can be far stronger than heroin. A tablet being sold as one thing can contain something completely different.

The warning signs include extreme drowsiness, pinpoint pupils, slow or noisy breathing, and blue lips. Pinpoint pupils means the black centres of the eyes look unusually tiny.

To any teenagers reading this: if a mate goes down, becomes unwell or is difficult to wake after taking something, ring 999 straight away. Do not put them to bed to sleep it off. Do not leave them alone and assume they’ll be fine in the morning. Do not wait hours because you’re frightened of your parents finding out, or worried about getting into trouble. Stay with them, tell the call handler what’s happening and anything you know about what they’ve taken, and follow their instructions.

That delay matters. While everyone is panicking and hoping someone will sleep it off, their breathing can become dangerously slow and their brain can be left without enough oxygen. Ringing immediately is looking after your mate, not grassing them up.

The police have said, in black and white: “Our priority is preserving life.”

Naloxone nasal spray can reverse the effects of an opioid overdose. You can get a free kit from Brightpath drug and alcohol service on Stockport Road, next to the launderette. Anyone can ask and no names are needed. The training takes about ten minutes. They’re open Monday to Friday, 10am–4pm, and until 7pm on Thursdays. Having naloxone does not replace ringing 999 — make the call first, then follow what the emergency call handler tells you.

Parents and carers, please have this conversation with your kids THIS week. Not after half term, not when you get round to it. It doesn’t need to be a massive lecture or an interrogation about what they and their friends are doing. Ask whether they’d know what to do if a friend became unwell. Make sure they know that ringing for help comes before everything else, and that they would never be in trouble with you for making that call.

I had the chat with my own 14-year-old over his tea last night. There were the expected eye rolls, but he did listen, and he asked me what pinpoint pupils meant. We shouldn’t assume they already know this stuff just because we do.

And please, slagging kids off helps nobody. Nor does piling onto their families. Scared kids are less likely to ring for help if all they can hear is how much trouble they’ll be in or how stupid everyone thinks they are. That’s the whole problem. We want them to make the call while someone can still be helped.

Please share this post, not just like it. Send it to your teenagers, put it in your family and friends’ group chats, and make sure the people around you know: if someone goes down, ring 999 immediately. Don’t put them to bed, don’t wait, and don’t let fear of getting into trouble cost someone their life.
